extracted.intended_audience: colonial administrators, planters, traders, and missionaries working in West Africa (late 19th/early 20th century context)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and policy guidance for recruiting, paying, training, and managing native labour on the West African coast, including which tribes suit which tasks and cautions about imported labour and missionary methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour problem must be studied and solved before West Africa can advance
rubrics_metrics.description: The labour problem is one that must be studied and solved before West Africa can advance much further than its present culture condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that labour supply and management are foundational to economic progress; climate and disease make this especially urgent. The passage frames labour as a prerequisite issue for any plantation or public-works expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on white labour; climate makes it unworkable
rubrics_metrics.description: The climate is such that the country cannot be worked by white labourers; and that this state of affairs will remain as it is until some true specific is discovered for malaria, ... or some radical change takes place in the nature of the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and planning should assume European labour is unsuitable due to malaria and other deadly fevers (including 'malarial typhoid' and 'blackwater'). Strategies must therefore focus on native labour solutions rather than importing white workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose native groups for tasks according to known aptitudes (Kruman, Accra, Sierra Leonian)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kruman...are the most important people of West Africa; the Kruman is as fine a ship-and-beach-man as you could reasonably wish for, but no good for plantation work. The Accra...a very fair artisan, cook, or clerk, but also no good for plantation work, except as an overseer. The Sierra Leonian is a poor artisan, an excellent clerk, or subordinate official, but so unreliable in the matter of honesty as to be nearly reliable to swindle any employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign roles by matching tribal/regional aptitudes: Krumen for ship/beach/stevedoring work; Accra (Basel Mission influence) for artisanal, cook, or clerical duties and overseerships; Sierra Leoneans for clerical/subordinate official roles but be cautious about trust/honesty issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use payment-in-goods as customary and often preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: In the circles of society I most mix with on the Coast--the mercantile marine and the trading--he is always paid in goods, in cloth, gin, guns, tobacco, gunpowder, etc., with little concessions to his individual fancy in the matter, for each of these articles has a known value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers commonly pay labourers in trade goods rather than cash; many labourers prefer and expect this. Adapt wage systems to local preferences (goods, rations, cloth) and be aware of variations (some pay in cash, some provide food and clothing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and respect end-of-service customs and anxieties
rubrics_metrics.description: The somewhat cumbrous wage the Kruboy gets at the end of his term of service, minus those things he has had on account and plus those things he has 'found,' is certainly a source of great worry to our friend. He obtains a box...and then he buys a padlock and locks his box of treasure up, hanging the key with his other ju-jus round his neck...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of tribal/customary expectations about savings, taxation by elders, and the importance of passage home; these affect behaviour, retention, and anxieties of labourers. Employers should anticipate customs (e.g., heavy tribal taxes or redistribution) when structuring wages and permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage labour by making them respect and like you; preserve a firm manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule is, make them respect you, and make them like you...to always preserve a firm manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective supervisors combine firmness and personal regard: be steady, authoritative, and also likeable. The author gives practical tips (e.g., say 'NO' rather than a polite request) and relates that some learn this quickly while others need time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat severely but not brutally; never show mistakes or allow over-familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to treat them brutally, in fact it does not pay to do so, but it is necessary to treat them severely, to keep a steady hand over them. Never let them become familiar, never let them see you have made a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid brutality; maintain discipline and authority without cruelty. If you make an order error, portray it as their fault in a controlled way to preserve authority (anecdotal management tactic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not nag Africans; nagging breeds sulkiness and non-cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: You should never nag an African, it only makes him bothered and then sulky, and when he's sulky he'll lie down and die to spite you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Micromanagement and constant nagging are counterproductive; they provoke passive resistance. The author criticises 'military' nagging-style management (ascribed to Germans) and advises restraint in supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing foreign labour—experiments have failed and mortality is high
rubrics_metrics.description: Several important authorities have advocated the importation of foreign labour into Africa. This seems to me to be a fatal error...The Congo Free State have imported...West Indian negroes...and Chinamen. In both cases the mortality has been terrible...and the experiment has therefore failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on imported labour (West Indians, Chinamen, Annamese) because of high mortality and poor adaptation to West African climate; historical cases demonstrate failure even when treatment varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop native labour locally through proper guidance and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Africa possesses in herself the most magnificent mass of labour material in the whole world, and surely if her children could build up...she should, under proper guidance and good management, be able to build up her own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in training and sensible management of local populations rather than importing outsiders. The Krumen example shows that training and employment practices can create reliable labour pools that others could emulate with 'common sense' regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical ship-and-shore vocational training is most useful and least harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Their first tutors were the slavers...Their next tutors were the traders...the two lessons he has learnt—ship and shore work—are the best that the white has so far taught the black, because unattended with the evil consequences that have followed the other lessons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise pragmatic, vocational instruction (cargo handling, ship skills, shore work) which enhance employability without some of the negative cultural impacts attributed to other forms of instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missionary methods can render natives 'useless' if they ignore difference of kind
rubrics_metrics.description: The Protestant English missionaries have had most to do with rendering the African useless...The bad effects...have come primarily from the failure of the missionary to recognise the difference between the African and themselves as being a difference not of degree but of kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trying to remake natives into copies of Europeans ('empty and refill' model); training and education should recognise cultural and psychological differences and be tailored rather than imposed. Missionary/education policy should account for different mental and social attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide decent rations and reasonable treatment—policy affects labour return rates
rubrics_metrics.description: The food given out by the German Government is the best Government rations given on the whole West Coast...When they have allowed me to have some of their native employes...I was much struck by the soundness and good quality of both rice and beef, and the rations they gave out to those Dahomeyans or Togolanders who revolted was so much more than they could, or cared to eat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good material treatment (adequate rations, reasonable conditions) improves retention and can counter criticisms of harsh regimes. Compare treatment practices across administrations to find effective standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect local contractual norms: 12-month engagements and passage guarantees
rubrics_metrics.description: Their habit of engaging for twelve-month terms of work and then returning to 'We country.' A trader who is satisfied with a boy gives him, when he leaves, a bit of paper telling the captain of any vessel that he will pay the boy's passage to his factory again, when he is willing to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise customary term lengths (often 12 months) and the social expectation of passage guarantees; use written notes/passages as local practice to ensure future recruitment and re-engagement.
